note: Tradeable commodities of the ~1500-1650 Age of Sail. `valueBand` and `baseValue` are GAME BALANCE numbers, not historical prices — see docs/WORLD_DATA.md. Enslaved people were the largest single item of Atlantic commerce in this period; that traffic is deliberately excluded from this list and will not be a tradeable good.

valueBands.1: bulk cargo — cheap by weight, profitable only in volume
valueBands.3: valuable — the backbone of a long-haul voyage
valueBands.4: rich — a hold of this pays for the ship
valueBands.5: treasure — priced per pound, guarded like bullion

goods.name: Black Pepper
goods.note: Malabar and Sumatra were the great sources; pepper was the bulk cargo that paid for the Carreira da India.

goods.name: Cloves
goods.note: Grew only on Ternate, Tidore and their neighbouring islets in the northern Moluccas before transplantation.

goods.name: Nutmeg
goods.note: The Banda islands were the world's only source; the VOC seized them outright in 1621.

goods.name: Mace
goods.note: The scarlet aril of the same Banda nutmeg fruit, scarcer than the nut itself and priced above it.

goods.name: Cinnamon
goods.note: The true cinnamon of Ceylon's western lowlands; Portugal and then the Dutch fought for the peeling monopoly.

goods.name: Ginger
goods.note: Malabar and Bengal, and from the 1520s a transplanted crop on Hispaniola and Jamaica.

goods.name: Cardamom
goods.note: The Cardamom Hills of the Western Ghats behind the Malabar pepper ports.

goods.name: Long Pepper
goods.note: The hotter catkin pepper of Bengal, sold beside the round Malabar berry since Roman times.

goods.name: Cubeb
goods.note: The tailed pepper of Java, sold by apothecaries as much as by cooks.

goods.name: Grains of Paradise
goods.note: The pungent seed of the Guinea coast that named the Grain Coast; a cheap stand-in for pepper.

goods.name: Cassia
goods.note: The thick cinnamon bark of south China and Tonkin, coarser and cheaper than the Ceylon peel.

goods.name: Turmeric
goods.note: The yellow root of India, dye and spice in one; every bazaar of the Indian Ocean priced it.

goods.name: Saffron
goods.note: La Mancha and Persian crocus threads, picked by hand; the dearest spice in the world by weight.

goods.name: Chillies
goods.note: The New World pepper the Portuguese carried to Goa, where it conquered every kitchen in a generation.

goods.name: Vanilla
goods.note: The cured orchid pod of the Totonac country behind Veracruz, drunk with chocolate in Mexico and Madrid.

goods.name: Aniseed
goods.note: Spanish and Apulian aniseed for comfits, cordials and the still-house.

goods.name: Cumin
goods.note: Egyptian and Gujarati cumin seed, a workhorse spice sold in sacks rather than caskets.

goods.name: Coriander
goods.note: Levantine and Spanish coriander seed, ballast-cheap and asked for everywhere.

goods.name: Galangal
goods.note: The ginger-like root of Siam and Champa, prized by apothecaries as far away as Europe.

goods.name: Star Anise
goods.note: The eight-pointed pod of the Tonkin borderlands, sweeter than aniseed and dearer.

goods.name: Allspice
goods.note: Jamaica pimento, tasting of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once; the island was its only source.

goods.name: Zedoary
goods.note: A bitter camphor-scented root of Ceylon and the Indies, sold to European apothecaries as a drug.

goods.name: Woollen Cloth
goods.note: England's broadcloth and kerseys, and Flemish and Florentine cloth, were Europe's chief export westward and east.

goods.name: Linen
goods.note: Brittany, Flanders, Silesia and Egypt; the ordinary cloth of shirts, sails and paper rag.

goods.name: Cotton Cloth
goods.note: Gujarati and Coromandel calicoes were the currency of the Indian Ocean, bought in India to buy spices elsewhere.

goods.name: Muslin
goods.note: The gossamer cottons of Dhaka and the Bengal delta, the finest woven cloth of the period.

goods.name: Chintz
goods.note: Painted and mordant-dyed Coromandel cottons; kalamkari from Machilipatnam and Pulicat.

goods.name: Silk Cloth
goods.note: Chinese damasks and satins, Persian brocades, and the woven silks of Bursa, Valencia and Lucca.

goods.name: Raw Silk
goods.note: Chinese and Persian filature silk; the Macau-Nagasaki run traded it for Japanese silver.

goods.name: Carpets
goods.note: Safavid Persia and Ottoman Anatolia; carried west overland to Aleppo and by sea from Bandar Abbas.

goods.name: Ramie Cloth
goods.note: Korean mosi, a fine summer bast cloth, among the goods traded through the Busan Waegwan to Tsushima.

goods.name: Says & Serges
goods.note: The light "new draperies" of Flanders and Zeeland that undercut old broadcloth in every warm market.

goods.name: Velvet
goods.note: Genoese and Venetian silk velvet, the cloth of cardinals and council chambers.

goods.name: Lace
goods.note: Venetian needle lace and Flemish bobbin lace, worth more than the linen it trimmed.

goods.name: Tapestries
goods.note: Brussels and Oudenaarde hangings sold through Antwerp; a single suite could furnish a palace.

goods.name: Batik Cloth
goods.note: Wax-resist patterned cottons of Java, traded through the pasisir ports alongside Indian cloth.

goods.name: Raffia Cloth
goods.note: The palm-fibre cloth of Kongo and Loango, so trusted it passed as money on the coast.

goods.name: Barkcloth
goods.note: Beaten bark tapa of the Pacific islands, patterned and traded from canoe to canoe.

goods.name: Camlets
goods.note: The watered mohair cloth of Angora goats, carried down to Smyrna for the Levant Company ships.

goods.name: Bengal Quilts
goods.note: The embroidered colchas of Satgaon, stitched in silk on cotton; a Portuguese favourite from the first.

goods.name: Kashmir Shawls
goods.note: Goat-down shawls woven in Kashmir and carried down to the Gujarat and Sind ports; a season each on the loom.

goods.name: Fustian
goods.note: The cotton-linen workhorse cloth of Milan and Augsburg, shipped out through Genoa and the Elbe.

goods.name: Gold Thread
goods.note: Gilt-silver thread of Genoa and Cyprus for brocades and church work, sold by the spool like treasure.

goods.name: Knitted Stockings
goods.note: Jersey and English worsted stockings, knitted by the thousand dozen for every market in Europe.

goods.name: Felt Hats
goods.note: Beaver felt hats of London and Normandy — the reason the beaver pelts crossed the Atlantic at all.

goods.name: Gold
goods.note: Akan gold through Elmina, Zimbabwean gold through Sofala, and New Granada placer gold through Cartagena.

goods.name: Silver
goods.note: Potosi and Zacatecas fed Seville and, via the Manila galleon, China; Japan's Iwami mines fed the same demand.

goods.name: Copper
goods.note: Swedish Falun and Hungarian copper in Europe; Japanese bar copper became a major VOC export good.

goods.name: Tin
goods.note: Cornwall in Europe, and the Malay peninsula and Bangka in Asia, where tin ingots served as money.

goods.name: Iron
goods.note: Biscayan and Swedish bar iron, and the trade iron bartered by the bundle on the African and American coasts.

goods.name: Lead
goods.note: Derbyshire and Polish lead in pigs and rolls, for shot, roofs and the assay office.

goods.name: Quicksilver
goods.note: Mercury of Almaden, Idria and Huancavelica; without it no silver amalgam, so crowns fought over every flask.

goods.name: Wootz Steel
goods.note: The crucible steel cakes of the Deccan that Damascus smiths forged into watered blades.

goods.name: Muskets
goods.note: Sakai matchlocks and Low Countries muskets; a chest of them opened doors on every coast.

goods.name: Cannon
goods.note: Wealden cast-iron guns and Swedish pieces; a strategic export every state tried and failed to embargo.

goods.name: Brassware & Manillas
goods.note: Nuremberg and Aachen basins, kettles and manilla bracelets — the currency goods of the Guinea trade.

goods.name: Pewterware
goods.note: English pewter plates and flagons, the everyday shine of every tavern from Danzig to Barbados.

goods.name: Copper Cash
goods.note: Strings of Chinese cash, shipped as money itself to Japan and Java where the coin was current.

goods.name: Nuremberg Smallwares
goods.note: Knives, needles, mirrors and bells by the barrel — the small iron goods every factor bartered.

goods.name: Armour
goods.note: Milanese corslets and morions shipped through Genoa; a fading trade, but princes still paid.

goods.name: Gunpowder
goods.note: Corned powder from the Amsterdam, London and Venetian mills; every fort and fleet ran dry without it.

goods.name: Porcelain
goods.note: Jingdezhen blue-and-white shipped through Canton and Macau; the kraak ware the Dutch took from Portuguese carracks.

goods.name: Lacquerware
goods.note: Japanese and Ryukyuan urushi ware, and Vietnamese and Korean lacquer, prized as cabinet goods in Europe.

goods.name: Glassware
goods.note: Murano cristallo and mirrors, and the fine glass of Barcelona; Venice guarded the craft as a state secret.

goods.name: Pearls
goods.note: The Gulf banks off Bahrain and Julfar, the Gulf of Mannar between India and Ceylon, and Venezuela's Cubagua.

goods.name: Diamonds
goods.note: Golconda stones sold through Machilipatnam, and the Landak diamonds of Borneo; cut and set in Antwerp and Goa.

goods.name: Ivory
goods.note: African elephant ivory from the Guinea, Kongo and Swahili coasts, carved in Lisbon, Dieppe and Gujarat.

goods.name: Ambergris
goods.note: Found washed up on Indian Ocean and Atlantic island shores; a fixative that made perfume scent last.

goods.name: Musk
goods.note: Himalayan and Chinese musk pods, carried down to Canton and Macau and sold by the ounce.

goods.name: Coral
goods.note: Red coral fished off Sardinia, Corsica and the Barbary coast, worked at Genoa and Livorno and sold into India.

goods.name: Amber
goods.note: The Samland coast of Prussia held a ducal monopoly; worked at Konigsberg and Gdansk, sold as far as China.

goods.name: Frankincense
goods.note: Dhofar in southern Arabia and the Somali coast behind Berbera, shipped through Aden and Mocha.

goods.name: Myrrh
goods.note: The same Arabian and Somali dry country as frankincense; used as incense, medicine and embalming resin.

goods.name: Rubies
goods.note: The stones of the Mogok mines above Pegu, carried out through the Burma ports sewn into clothing.

goods.name: Emeralds
goods.note: Muzo emeralds of New Granada, greener than anything the old world had cut.

goods.name: Carnelian & Agate
goods.note: The banded stones of Cambay, cut and polished there into beads for three continents.

goods.name: Printed Books
goods.note: The presses of Venice and the Plantin house at Antwerp; bales of books moved like any other cloth.

goods.name: Paper
goods.note: Ligurian reams, Chinese bamboo paper and Korean hanji; the clerks of the world never had enough.

goods.name: Tortoiseshell
goods.note: Hawksbill shell from the Ryukyus, the Visayas and the Caribbean, worked into combs and inlay.

goods.name: Mastic
goods.note: The resin tears of Chios, chewed in the harems and guarded by the Ottomans on pain of death.

goods.name: Civet
goods.note: Ethiopian civet paste scraped by the ounce, the base note of every great perfume house.

goods.name: Rosewater
goods.note: Distilled roses of Shiraz and Damascus, shipped in glass carboys packed in straw.

goods.name: Clocks & Instruments
goods.note: Nuremberg and Augsburg clockwork and Dutch instruments; the Jesuits opened Peking with such gifts.

goods.name: Paintings
goods.note: Antwerp's picture market sold devotional panels and landscapes by the crate, sight unseen.

goods.name: Bezoar Stones
goods.note: Stones from the stomachs of goats and porcupines, sworn to defeat any poison; Goa even made its own.

goods.name: Rhinoceros Horn
goods.note: African and Asian horn, carved into cups that were said to sweat at the touch of poison.

goods.name: Lapis Lazuli
goods.note: The blue stone of Badakhshan, ground in Europe into ultramarine dearer than gold leaf.

goods.name: Turquoise
goods.note: Nishapur turquoise of Persia, the sky-blue stone of daggers and turban jewels.

goods.name: Folding Fans
goods.note: Kyoto folding fans shipped through Sakai; Europe copied the idea and never the finish.

goods.name: Silverware & Plate
goods.note: Augsburg workshops and Seville shops turned bullion into cups and salvers that travelled as gifts of state.

goods.name: Majolica
goods.note: Tin-glazed ware of Montelupo and Manises, the bright pottery of every Mediterranean table.

goods.name: Celadon Ware
goods.note: Sawankhalok green ware out of Siam and Korean bowls the Japanese tea masters ruined themselves for.

goods.name: Rhenish Stoneware
goods.note: Salt-glazed jugs and bellarmines of the Rhine kilns, shipped down to every North Sea harbour.

goods.name: Martaban Jars
goods.note: The great glazed storage jars of Martaban, prized from Japan to Arabia for keeping water sweet.

goods.name: Trade Beads
goods.note: Murano conterie and Dutch beads by the barrel, the small change of the Guinea and fur trades.

goods.name: Sea Charts & Globes
goods.note: Waggoners, portolans and globes from the Low Countries presses; a good rutter was worth a cargo.

goods.name: Ink & Brushes
goods.note: Huizhou ink sticks and Korean brushes, the tools of every yamen and academy.

goods.name: Sword Blades
goods.note: Japanese blades shipped to China by the thousand, with Toledo and Solingen steel for the western trade.

goods.name: Venice Treacle
goods.note: The sixty-ingredient cure-all compounded in public in Venice and faked everywhere else.

goods.name: Parrots & Monkeys
goods.note: Live curiosities of Brazil and Guinea; a talking bird paid a sailor better than his wages.

goods.name: Gyrfalcons
goods.note: White Iceland falcons, a trade so royal the Danish crown kept it to itself.

goods.name: Bird-of-Paradise Plumes
goods.note: Legless skins from the Aru islands, sold in Europe as birds that lived their whole lives on the wing.

goods.name: Wheat
goods.note: Sicilian and Egyptian wheat, and the Vistula grain fleets out of Gdansk; the great bulk trade of every sea.

goods.name: Rice
goods.note: Bengal, Siam, Java and Kanara fed the rice-deficit ports of the Indian Ocean and the Moluccas.

goods.name: Sugar
goods.note: Madeira and Sao Tome first, then the Pernambuco and Bahia mills and, from the 1640s, Barbados.

goods.name: Salt
goods.note: Setubal, the Bay of Bourgneuf and the Punta de Araya pans; without it no fishery or long voyage was possible.

goods.name: Olive Oil
goods.note: Andalusia, Apulia and the Levant; used as much for soap-making and cloth fulling as for food.

goods.name: Wine
goods.note: Bordeaux claret, Canary sack, Madeira and Cretan malmsey — the grape wines every northern fleet came south for.

goods.name: Dried & Salt Fish
goods.note: Newfoundland and Iceland cod and Norwegian stockfish; the protein that provisioned Catholic Europe and its ships.

goods.name: Herring
goods.note: The North Sea and Baltic fishery, gutted and barrelled at sea by the Dutch buss fleets.

goods.name: Cheese
goods.note: Holland's Edam and Gouda rounds kept at sea for months and provisioned fleets on every ocean route.

goods.name: Salt Meat
goods.note: Irish and Baltic barrelled beef and pork; also the hide-and-tallow cattle economy of the Plata and Hispaniola.

goods.name: Coffee
goods.note: Grown in the Yemeni highlands and shipped through Mocha, its only outlet until the 18th century.

goods.name: Tea
goods.note: Fujian and Zhejiang leaf; the first Dutch shipment reached Europe from Java in 1610.

goods.name: Cacao
goods.note: Soconusco, Guayaquil and the Venezuelan coast; drunk in New Spain long before the Spanish court took it up.

goods.name: Raisins & Currants
goods.note: Malaga raisins, Ionian currants and the sun-dried vine fruit of the Aegean, shipped north by the shipload.

goods.name: Rye
goods.note: The black bread grain of the Baltic, floated down the Vistula and sold by the last; Amsterdam lived on it.

goods.name: Barley
goods.note: Malting barley of the northern firths and sounds; the brewhouse bought all of it.

goods.name: Beer
goods.note: Hamburg and Danzig hopped beer and English ale, safer than water and shipped by the hundred barrels.

goods.name: Sake
goods.note: The rice brew of Itami and Nada, casked at Osaka for every castle town on the seaway.

goods.name: Rum
goods.note: The kill-devil spirit of the Barbados cane mills, aged into currency in every buccaneer port.

goods.name: Brandy
goods.note: Burnt wine of the Charente and Gironde, distilled so it could survive any voyage and improve for it.

goods.name: Arrack
goods.note: Palm and rice spirit of Batavia, Ceylon and Goa; the sailor’s punch on every eastern voyage.

goods.name: Butter
goods.note: Irish and Dutch salted butter in firkins, victualling fleets and plantations alike.

goods.name: Honey
goods.note: Lithuanian forest honey and Barbary honey, the sweetener of everyone the sugar ships passed by.

goods.name: Dates
goods.note: Basra and Oman dates pressed into baskets, the cheap sweet cargo of every Gulf and Barbary sailing.

goods.name: Figs
goods.note: Smyrna and Malaga figs, drummed and shipped north for winter tables.

goods.name: Lemons & Oranges
goods.note: Sicilian and Valencian citrus; ship captains bought them without knowing why they kept crews standing.

goods.name: Almonds
goods.note: Andalusian, Apulian and Sous almonds, the marzipan and banquet nut of Europe.

goods.name: Coconuts & Copra
goods.note: Nut, oil and coir from the same palm; the Indian Ocean’s tree of everything.

goods.name: Sago
goods.note: Palm-pith flour of the eastern islands, the bread of the spice country.

goods.name: Maize
goods.note: The Indian corn of the Americas, already feeding garrisons and slave ships on both shores.

goods.name: Cassava Flour
goods.note: Farinha de guerra, the toasted root flour that provisioned every Brazil and Angola voyage.

goods.name: Caviar
goods.note: Pressed sturgeon roe of the Black Sea and Volga, barrelled for Italy since Genoese Kaffa.

goods.name: Salt Tuna
goods.note: The almadraba tunny of the straits, netted at the season and salted down by the thousand.

goods.name: Soy Sauce
goods.note: Brewed soy of Japan, casked at Nagasaki; the Dutch carried it as far as Batavia and beyond.

goods.name: Ghee
goods.note: Clarified butter of Gujarat and Sind, shipped in jars wherever Indian crews and kitchens went.

goods.name: Sesame Oil
goods.note: The lamp and cooking oil of Egypt and Bengal, pressed where the olive will not grow.

goods.name: Palm Oil
goods.note: The red cooking oil of the Guinea coast, bought by every factory to feed its own people.

goods.name: Edible Birds’ Nests
goods.note: Swiftlet nests gathered from cliff caves for the soup kitchens of Canton; worth their weight in silver.

goods.name: Shark Fin
goods.note: Dried fins from the eastern seas, bound for the Chinese banquet trade.

goods.name: Trepang
goods.note: Smoked sea cucumber of the Makassar praus, fished as far as the dry south land for Chinese kitchens.

goods.name: Dried Abalone
goods.note: Diver-gathered abalone of Jeju and Kyushu, dried hard and prized in China above fresh pearl.

goods.name: Dried Seaweed
goods.note: Kelp and laver of the Korea Strait, dried on every foreshore and eaten in every kitchen.

goods.name: Palm Sugar
goods.note: Jaggery boiled from palm sap, the everyday sweet of Bengal and the Indies.

goods.name: Molasses
goods.note: The mill syrup left when sugar is struck; sold cheap, and the seed of every rum still.

goods.name: Tamarind
goods.note: The sour pod of India, packed in jars as ship’s physic and kitchen souring both.

goods.name: Hazelnuts
goods.note: The filbert groves of the Pontic shore behind Trebizond, shipped west since antiquity.

goods.name: Pistachios
goods.note: Aleppo and Persian pistachios, the banquet nut of the Ottoman and Safavid courts.

goods.name: Dried Lychees
goods.note: The Fujian orchard fruit, dried to raisins of the south and shipped up the whole China coast.

goods.name: Tobacco
goods.note: Virginia from 1614, Trinidad and the Orinoco earlier still, and Ottoman Latakia by the 17th century.

goods.name: Indigo
goods.note: Gujarat's Sarkhej and Bengal indigo displaced European woad as the blue dye of the wool trade.

goods.name: Cochineal
goods.note: The dried insect of Oaxaca, worth more by weight than most spices and second only to silver in New Spain's exports.

goods.name: Brazilwood
goods.note: The red dyewood that named Brazil, cut along the coast the Portuguese found it on.

goods.name: Logwood
goods.note: Campeche and the Yucatan lagoons; a black and purple dyewood that later drew English cutters and buccaneers.

goods.name: Alum
goods.note: The papal alum of Tolfa and the Anatolian alum of the old Phocaea works: the mordant that fixed dye to cloth.

goods.name: Saltpetre
goods.note: Bihar and the Ganges plain; refined at Patna and shipped down the Hugli as the powder trade's key ingredient.

goods.name: Sulphur
goods.note: Sicily, Iceland and the Japanese and Ryukyuan volcanoes; the other half of gunpowder.

goods.name: Hides
goods.note: Plata and Hispaniola cattle hides, Irish and Barbary skins; the raw side of every leather trade.

goods.name: Furs
goods.note: Canadian beaver through Tadoussac and the Hudson, and Russian sable and ermine through Arkhangelsk.

goods.name: Beeswax
goods.note: Baltic, Barbary and Guinea beeswax for church candles and seals; a steady cargo on every coast.

goods.name: Raw Cotton
goods.note: Gujarat, western Anatolia, Cyprus and the Levant, spun in India and, increasingly, in Europe.

goods.name: Raw Wool
goods.note: Castilian merino shipped from Bilbao to Flanders, and English wool before the cloth trade absorbed it.

goods.name: Gum Arabic
goods.note: Acacia gum of the Senegal river marts, indispensable to dyers, printers and apothecaries.

goods.name: Sandalwood
goods.note: The fragrant heartwood of Timor and the lesser Sundas, burned in Chinese temples and carved for the gods.

goods.name: Ginseng
goods.note: Korean mountain root, the highest-value good of the Joseon-Tsushima trade, sold on to Chinese physicians.

goods.name: Horses
goods.note: Arabian, Persian and Barbary horses shipped from Hormuz and Aden to Goa and the Deccan; the Portuguese taxed the trade hard.

goods.name: Potash
goods.note: Forest ash of Poland and Muscovy, burned by the ton for the soap, glass and dye trades.

goods.name: Tallow
goods.note: Rendered fat of the Russian and Plata herds; candles, soap and greased rigging all began here.

goods.name: Woad
goods.note: The blue dye balls of Toulouse and the Azores, fighting a losing war against Indian indigo.

goods.name: Madder
goods.note: The red root of Anatolia and Zeeland, the everyday scarlet of the cloth trade.

goods.name: Lac & Shellac
goods.note: The insect resin of Pegu and Bengal: scarlet dye, sealing wax and the polish on every cabinet.

goods.name: Annatto
goods.note: The orange seed paste of the Amazon and the Main, sold to dyers and Dutch cheese makers alike.

goods.name: Orchil
goods.note: Purple lichen dye scraped from Atlantic island rocks; the reason crowns quarrelled over bare cliffs.

goods.name: Henna
goods.note: The leaf dye of the oases, sold through the Barbary ports to half the world’s markets.

goods.name: Borneo Camphor
goods.note: Crystal camphor of Barus and Borneo, worth many times the Chinese sort; medicine, incense and embalming.

goods.name: Benzoin
goods.note: The sweet resin of Sumatra and Siam, burned as incense from Lisbon to Nagasaki.

goods.name: Aloeswood
goods.note: Agarwood of the Champa hills; a single resinous log could ransom the ship that carried it.

goods.name: Dragon’s Blood
goods.note: The red resin of Socotra’s dragon trees, sold as medicine, varnish and pigment.

goods.name: Socotrine Aloes
goods.note: Bitter aloe juice dried on Socotra, the purge in every ship surgeon’s chest.

goods.name: Myrobalans
goods.note: The tanning and dyeing fruit of India, bought by the bale for leather and ink.

goods.name: Sappanwood
goods.note: The red dyewood of Siam; junk after junk carried it to Japan, where it paid for silver.

goods.name: Red Sanders
goods.note: The Coromandel red wood, cousin to sappan, cut in the Palakonda hills for the dye vats.

goods.name: Camwood
goods.note: The red dyewood of the Guinea and Kongo forests, ground to a paste for cloth and skin alike.

goods.name: Ebony
goods.note: The black heartwood of Ceylon and the Mozambique coast, turned into cabinets and crucifixes.

goods.name: Rattan
goods.note: The climbing cane of the Indies: cables, baskets and chairs from one forest vine.

goods.name: Opium
goods.note: Malwa and Patna opium, already a staple of the Indian Ocean drug trade the Portuguese taxed at Goa.

goods.name: Areca Nuts
goods.note: The betel nut of Ceylon and Malabar, chewed from Arabia to the Moluccas; a bulk trade in its own right.

goods.name: Kola Nuts
goods.note: The bitter caffeine nut of the Guinea forest, traded north by caravan and along the coast by canoe.

goods.name: Sarsaparilla
goods.note: The Honduras root sworn by half of Europe to cure the pox; apothecaries paid whatever was asked.

goods.name: Sassafras
goods.note: The ague-tree bark of Virginia and Florida, the first paying cargo the English colonies ever found.

goods.name: Senna
goods.note: The purging leaf of the upper Nile country, sold through Cairo to every apothecary in Europe.

goods.name: Chinese Rhubarb
goods.note: The dried medicinal root of the Chinese northwest, dearer in Europe than cinnamon.

goods.name: China Root
goods.note: The smilax root the Portuguese carried from Macau as the new cure for the French disease.

goods.name: Mother-of-Pearl
goods.note: Nacre shell of the Gulf and Sulu banks, cut for inlay in Gujarat, Canton and Kyoto.

goods.name: Cowrie Shells
goods.note: Maldive shells shipped by the ton through Ceylon and Bengal; the small money of three continents.

goods.name: Chank Shells
goods.note: The sacred conch of the Mannar banks, sawn into bangles for Bengal.

goods.name: Coir
goods.note: Coconut husk fibre of Malabar and the isles; the sewn ships of the Indian Ocean are stitched with it.

goods.name: Gallnuts
goods.note: Aleppo and Kurdish oak galls, the heart of every good black ink and dye.

goods.name: Jesuit’s Bark
goods.note: The fever bark of the Peruvian montana, carried to Rome by the Jesuits from the 1630s.

goods.name: Ostrich Feathers
goods.note: Saharan plumes carried to the coast by caravan, nodding on every helmet and hat in Europe.

goods.name: Sponges
goods.note: Diver-gathered sponges of the Aegean and Lycian coasts, sold from surgeons’ shops to stables.

goods.name: Whalebone
goods.note: The springy jaw plates of the Greenland whale: stays, whips and window panes of the north.

goods.name: Sealskins
goods.note: Oiled skins of the northern hunt, waterproof before anything else was.

goods.name: Walrus Ivory
goods.note: Morse teeth of the White Sea and Spitsbergen hunts, carved where elephant ivory never reached.

goods.name: Narwhal Horn
goods.note: The spiral tusk sold in Europe as unicorn horn, proof against poison and priced like a province.

goods.name: Eiderdown
goods.note: Nest down of the eider duck, gathered on the skerries; the warmest thing the north ever sold.

goods.name: Sea Coal
goods.note: Tyne and Forth coal carried coastwise and across the North Sea; the fuel of salt pans and smithies.

goods.name: Marble
goods.note: Carrara blocks and sawn slabs, shipped from the Ligurian shore to palaces and altars abroad.

goods.name: Cork
goods.note: Stripped oak bark of Portugal: floats, soles and the stoppers in every bottle.

goods.name: Copal
goods.note: Incense and varnish resin, dug fossil on the Swahili coast and tapped fresh in New Spain.

goods.name: Tiger Skins
goods.note: Joseon tiger and leopard skins, the prestige export the Japanese daimyo paid silver for.

goods.name: Isinglass
goods.note: Sturgeon bladder glue of the Volga fisheries, the finest clarifier and adhesive money could buy.

goods.name: Russia Leather
goods.note: Birch-oil dressed yuft, red and waterproof; bookbinders and saddlers knew it by smell alone.

goods.name: Morocco Leather
goods.note: Goatskin dressed soft and scarlet in Fez and Marrakesh; the binding of every fine library.

goods.name: Balsam of Peru
goods.note: The dark healing balsam of the Guatemalan coast, shipped through New Spain under a misleading name.

goods.name: Jalap
goods.note: The purging root of the Veracruz hills, a New World drug every European apothecary stocked.

goods.name: Vicuña Wool
goods.note: The finest fleece in the world, combed from wild Andean vicuña and reserved once for the Inca.

goods.name: Guaiacum
goods.note: The iron-heavy holy wood of Hispaniola, sold as a pox cure and turned into blocks and mortars.

goods.name: Verdigris
goods.note: The green copper pigment of Montpellier, raised on wine lees and sold by the barrel.

goods.name: Cobalt Blue
goods.note: The Persian ore behind Mohammedan blue; Jingdezhen’s best porcelain was painted with it.

goods.name: Gamboge
goods.note: The golden gum of the Cambodian forests, at once a pigment and a violent purge.

goods.name: Safflower
goods.note: The rouge and dye thistle of Egypt and India, the poor man’s saffron.

goods.name: Catechu
goods.note: Cutch, the dark tanning extract of Pegu and India, boiled from heartwood and sold in cakes.

goods.name: War Elephants
goods.note: Ceylon and Pegu elephants, shipped standing to the courts of India; the grandest cargo afloat.

goods.name: Spikenard
goods.note: The aromatic root of the high Himalaya, carried down the Ganges as it had been since Rome.

goods.name: Asafoetida
goods.note: The foul-smelling gum of Persia and Afghanistan that Indian cooking cannot do without.

goods.name: Balm of Mecca
goods.note: The true balsam of the Hejaz gardens, so scarce that most of what sold under the name was not it.

goods.name: Linseed
goods.note: Baltic flax seed, crushed for the oil that binds every painter’s colour and printer’s ink.

goods.name: Hops
goods.note: The bitter cone that turned ale into beer; grown in Brabant and the Elbe country, sold by the sack.

goods.name: Soap
goods.note: Olive-oil soap of Marseille, Aleppo and Venice, boxed and shipped as a finished ware.

goods.name: Vermilion
goods.note: The scarlet mercury pigment, made in China and Holland and sold by the pound to painters and printers.

goods.name: Timber
goods.note: Baltic oak and fir, wainscot and clapboard; the planking trade no shipyard could live without.

goods.name: Masts & Spars
goods.note: Riga and Norwegian mast pine, and later New England white pine; a strategic good every navy competed for.

goods.name: Tar & Pitch
goods.note: Finnish and Swedish pine tar through Stockholm and Turku; without it no hull or rigging stayed sound.

goods.name: Hemp & Cordage
goods.note: Riga and Russian hemp for European rope-walks; the rigging of every fleet began as this fibre.

goods.name: Flax & Sailcloth
goods.note: Baltic and Dutch flax woven into the canvas that every ocean-going ship carried in bolts as spare sail.

goods.name: Whale & Train Oil
goods.note: Basque and later Dutch and English whaling off Spitsbergen; lamp oil, soap stock and cloth dressing.

goods.name: Teak
goods.note: The shipbuilding wood of Malabar and Pegu that laughs at worm and weather; every eastern yard ran on it.

goods.name: Rosin & Turpentine
goods.note: Pine gum of the Landes and the Baltic forests, for caulkers, coopers and fiddlers alike.

goods.name: Cedar Timber
goods.note: Bermuda cedar built the fastest small hulls afloat; Lebanon’s groves were already legend.

goods.name: Mangrove Poles
goods.note: Boriti poles of the Swahili creeks, the roof timber of every treeless Gulf town.

goods.name: Manila Hemp
goods.note: Banana-fibre cordage of the Philippines; the galleons rigged themselves with it.
